The Afrikaners, the people of Dutch descent in South Africa, founded two republics in the 1850s: the Transvaal and the Orange Free State, with Dutch as the official language, though a strong influence of English was present also here (Mesthrie 2002: 17).
The idea prevalent in older days that most Dutch grammatical norms are valid for Afrikaans as well has rapidly been fading and the huge influence of English is now recognized (Donaldson 1993: xv).

Between 1784 and 1808 the import of slaves was the biggest, by then mainly taken from the east of Africa and Madagascar (Roberge 2002: 81), resulting in the most diverse slave population known (Shell 1994: 11).

After precious metals had been found in the 1860s, the British took over the Transvaal in 1877, which reinforced Afrikaner nationalism, and this was followed by two wars between Afrikaners and British, of which the latter was won by the British (Mesthrie 2002: 17).

In 1910 the Union of South Africa was founded, with English and Dutch as the official languages (the latter being replaced in 1925 by Afrikaans), as the Afrikaners strongly rejected the Anglicization attempts of the British (Mesthrie 2002: 18).
The most original indigenous people of South Africa are those referred to as “Khoesan”, who lived as hunter-gatherers or livestock herders (Mesthrie 2002: 13).
After heavy protests against white domination in the 1970s and 1980s, in which many lives were lost, South Africa became a democracy in 1994.
